ety.text: Borrowed from the name of the Venetian Ghetto, whose etymology and original source language is uncertain. Compare Italian ghetto.

senses.d: An (often walled) area of a city in which Jews are concentrated by force and law. (Used particularly of areas in medieval Italy and in Nazi-controlled Europe.)
ex: Established by the Germans in October 1940, the Warsaw Ghetto was the largest Jewish ghetto in German-occupied Europe.
senses.zh: 猶太人居住區；猶太區；隔都

senses.d: An (often impoverished) area of a city inhabited predominantly by members of a specific nationality, ethnicity, or race.
ex: Charlestown would also become one of Boston's three large Irish ghettoes.
By 1960 the growth and development of Chicago's black areas of residence confirmed the existence of the city's second ghetto.
senses.zh: 猶太人居住區；猶太區；隔都

senses.d: An area in which people who are distinguished by sharing something other than ethnicity concentrate or are concentrated.
An isolated, self-contained, segregated subsection, area or field of interest; often of minority or specialist interest.
ex: Invent is undoubtedly the wrong word, but the push from government was crucial in getting the Internet out of its academic ghetto.
senses.zh: 猶太人居住區；猶太區；隔都

senses.d: Of or relating to a ghetto or to ghettos in general.
Unseemly and indecorous or of low quality; cheap; shabby, crude.
ex: My apartment's so ghetto, the rats and cockroaches filed a complaint with the city!
I like to drive ghetto cars; if they break down you can just abandon them and pick up a new one!

senses.d: Characteristic of the style, speech, or behavior of residents of a predominantly black or other ghetto in the United States.
ex: I beat up my kid's principal. Can you get any more ghetto than that?

senses.d: Having been raised in a ghetto in the United States.
To confine (a specified group of people) to a ghetto.
ex: This is, in brief, a part of the story of the ghettoing of a large segment of Denver's Negro population.

area of a city where people of an ethnic group are concentrated

ety.text: Borrowed from Venetan ghèto (“foundry”). Alternatively a clipping of borghetto, diminutive of borgo (“village”). Initially used of the areas Jews were concentrated, later extended to concentrations of other ethnicities and then non-ethnic groups.
From Andalusian Arabic الجمع (al-jámaʕ), from Arabic جَمْع (jamʕ).
